clause_heading: Protection of life and personal liberty
chunk_text:
Constitution of India, 1950 · Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty)

No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. This guarantees fundamental human dignity, privacy, and right to legal representation.

clause_heading: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
chunk_text:
Constitution of India, 1950 · Article 22 (Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases)

(1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.
(2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.
(3) Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention.

clause_heading: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account
chapter: Chapter XVII: Penalties in case of Dishonour of Certain Cheques
chunk_text:
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Section 138 (Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account)

Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both:
Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless - 
(a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier;
(b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and
(c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.

clause_heading: Cognizance of offences and limitation period
chapter: Chapter XVII: Penalties in case of Dishonour of Certain Cheques
chunk_text:
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 · Section 142 (Cognizance of offences and limitation period)

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - 
(a) no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 138 except upon a complaint, in writing, made by the payee or, as the case may be, the holder in due course of the cheque;
(b) such complaint is made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138:
Provided that the cognizance of a complaint may be taken by the Court after the prescribed period, if the complainant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not making a complaint within such period;
(c) no court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try any offence punishable under section 138.
(2) The offence under section 138 shall be inquired into and tried only by a court within whose local jurisdiction - 
(a) if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course, as the case may be, maintains the account, is situated; or
(b) if the cheque is presented for payment by the payee or holder in due course, otherwise through an account, the branch of the drawee bank where the drawer maintains the account, is situated.

clause_heading: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 318(4) (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property)

(1) Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to 'cheat'.
(4) Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

clause_heading: Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty
chapter: Chapter V: Offences Against Woman and Child
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 85 (Husband or relative of husband subjecting woman to cruelty)

Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. Cruelty includes willful conduct likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury, or harassment with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for dowry or property.

clause_heading: Punishment for murder and mob lynching
chapter: Chapter VI: Offences Affecting the Human Body
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 103 (Punishment for murder and mob lynching)

(1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(2) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

clause_heading: Theft and community service for petty theft
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 · Section 303(2) (Theft and community service for petty theft)

Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both:
Provided that in cases of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and a person is convicted for the first time, upon return of the stolen property or payment of the value thereof, the court may award punishment of community service.

clause_heading: Information in cognizable cases (FIR, Zero FIR & e-FIR)
chapter: Chapter XIII: Information to the Police and their Powers to Investigate
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 173 (Information in cognizable cases (FIR, Zero FIR & e-FIR))

(1) Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may prescribe in this behalf:
Provided that information may be given electronically (e-FIR), and such information shall be taken on record by the police officer, subject to the condition that the informant shall sign the same within three days before the First Information Report is formally registered:
Provided further that irrespective of the area where the offence was committed, information may be given to any police station, and such police station shall register the same as a 'Zero FIR' and transfer it immediately to the jurisdictional police station having authority over the place of offence.
(2) A copy of the information as recorded under sub-section (1) shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant or the person who gave the information.
(3) If police refuse to record information, the aggrieved person may send the substance of such information in writing and by post to the Superintendent of Police concerned, or approach the Magistrate under Section 175(3).

clause_heading: Notice of appearance before police officer and safeguards against arrest
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 35 (Notice of appearance before police officer and safeguards against arrest)

(1) The police officer may, in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1) of section 35, issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence, to appear before him or at such other place as may be specified in the notice.
(3) Where such notice is issued to any person, it shall be the duty of that person to comply with the terms of the notice.
Provided that no arrest shall be made without prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police where the offence is punishable with imprisonment for less than three years and the person is an infirm person or over sixty years of age.

clause_heading: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail)
chapter: Chapter XXXV: Provisions as to Bail and Bonds
chunk_text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 · Section 482 (Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest (Anticipatory Bail))

Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail; and that Court may, after considering the nature and gravity of accusation, the antecedents of the applicant, and the possibility of fleeing justice, direct that he be granted anticipatory bail subject to conditions including making himself available for interrogation.

chunk_text:
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Repealed) · Section 420 (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property)

Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person... shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. [REPEALED: Operative replacement is Section 318(4) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023].

clause_heading: Rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee
chapter: Chapter V: Of Leases of Immovable Property
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 108 (Rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee)

In the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, the lessor and the lessee of immovable property, as against one another, respectively, possess the rights and are subject to the liabilities following:
(m) the lessee is bound to keep, and on the termination of the lease to restore, the property in as good condition as it was in at the time when he was put in possession, reasonable wear and tear and irresistible force excepted;
(q) on the termination of the lease, the lessee is bound to put the lessor into possession of the property.
Security deposits paid by tenant constitute trust funds held by lessor, repayable immediately upon vacant possession handover, subject only to deductions for actual verified damages beyond ordinary wear and tear.

clause_heading: Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract and notice to quit
chapter: Chapter V: Of Leases of Immovable Property
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 106 (Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract and notice to quit)

In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose (including residential tenancy) shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice.

clause_heading: Protection of tenants against eviction and refund of advance deposit
chapter: Chapter V: Control of Eviction of Tenants
chunk_text:
Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 · Section 27 (Protection of tenants against eviction and refund of advance deposit)

(1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by the Court, District Judge or Rent Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant, save as provided in this section.
(2) The landlord shall not claim or receive any premium or other like sum or any advance exceeding one month's rent in case of residential tenancy, and any excess deposit received shall be accounted for and refunded to the tenant upon handover of vacant possession.
(3) Where the landlord refuses to accept rent or fails to refund the security deposit within thirty days of tenant vacating the premises, the tenant may apply to the Rent Controller having territorial jurisdiction for summary adjudication and recovery.

clause_heading: Landlord's duty to keep the premises in good repair
chunk_text:
Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 · Section 14 (Landlord's duty to keep the premises in good repair)

Every landlord shall be bound to keep the premises in good and tenantable repair. If the landlord neglects or fails to make within thirty days after notice in writing, any repairs which he is bound to make, the tenant may make the same and deduct one-fourth of the rent of the year from the rent payable.

clause_heading: Manner in which complaint shall be made before District Commission (e-Daakhil)
chapter: Chapter IV: Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
chunk_text:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 · Section 35 (Manner in which complaint shall be made before District Commission (e-Daakhil))

(1) A complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by - 
(a) the consumer to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided;
(b) any recognized consumer association;
(c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest; or
(d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government.
(2) Every complaint filed under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied with such fee and in such manner as may be prescribed, including electronic filing through the e-Daakhil portal.
(3) The complaint shall be admitted within twenty-one days of filing, and notice issued to the opposite party to respond within thirty days (extendable by fifteen days). Limitation period for filing a complaint is two years from the date on which the cause of action arose under Section 69.

clause_heading: Return of amount and compensation for project delay
chapter: Chapter III: Rights and Duties of Allottees
chunk_text:
Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 · Section 18 (Return of amount and compensation for project delay)

If the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment, plot or building in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale or by the date specified therein, the promoter shall be liable on demand to the allottees, in case the allottee wishes to withdraw from the project, to return the amount received by him in respect of that apartment, with interest at such rate as may be prescribed, including compensation. If the allottee does not intend to withdraw, he shall be paid interest for every month of delay until possession is delivered.

clause_heading: Divorce by mutual consent and cooling-off period
chapter: Chapter IV: Nullity of Marriage and Divorce
chunk_text:
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 · Section 13B (Divorce by mutual consent and cooling-off period)

(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce may be presented to the district court by both the parties to a marriage together, on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved.
(2) On the motion of both the parties made not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition referred to in sub-section (1) and not later than eighteen months after the said date, the court shall, on being satisfied, after hearing the parties and after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, pass a decree of divorce:
Provided that the Supreme Court and High Courts have held that the six-month cooling-off period can be waived under appropriate conditions where all efforts of mediation have failed and parties have settled all maintenance, custody, and property claims.

clause_heading: Equal coparcenary rights of daughters in ancestral joint family property
chunk_text:
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 · Section 6 (Equal coparcenary rights of daughters in ancestral joint family property)

On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall - 
(a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son;
(b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son;
(c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son,
and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener:
Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation, including any partition or testamentary disposition of property, which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
clause_heading: Protection orders and right to reside in shared household
chapter: Chapter IV: Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Reliefs
chunk_text:
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 · Section 18 & 19 (Protection orders and right to reside in shared household)

The Magistrate may, after giving the aggrieved person and the respondent an opportunity of being heard and on being prima facie satisfied that domestic violence has taken place, pass a protection order prohibiting the respondent from committing acts of domestic violence, entering the workplace or residence of aggrieved person, or alienating shared assets. Under Section 19, the Magistrate may direct the respondent not to dispossess or disturb the possession of the aggrieved woman from the shared household, irrespective of whether she has any legal title in the property.

clause_heading: Agreement in restraint of trade, void
chunk_text:
Indian Contract Act, 1872 · Section 27 (Agreement in restraint of trade, void)

Every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Non-compete clauses operating post-employment are unenforceable under Indian law, except where statutory goodwill of a business is sold.

clause_heading: Three-year period of limitation for contracts, recovery of money and specific performance
chunk_text:
Limitation Act, 1963 · Article 54 & Schedule (Three-year period of limitation for contracts, recovery of money and specific performance)

For specific performance of a contract or recovery of money based on breach of contract, the period of limitation is three years from the date fixed for performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. After expiry of three years, the legal remedy in court is barred by limitation.

clause_heading: Disposal of request within thirty days and 48-hour life or liberty window
chunk_text:
Right to Information Act, 2005 · Section 7 (Disposal of request within thirty days and 48-hour life or liberty window)

The Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer shall, on receipt of a request under Section 6, as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of the receipt of the request, either provide the information on payment of such fee as may be prescribed or reject the request: Provided that where the information sought for concerns the life or liberty of a person, the same shall be provided within forty-eight hours of the receipt of the request.

act: Filing an FIR and Remedies if Police Refuse
section: Zero FIR & Magistrate Remedies under Section 173 BNSS
clause_heading: Zero FIR & Magistrate Remedies under Section 173 BNSS
chunk_text:
Citizen Procedural Guide: Filing an FIR and Remedies if Police Refuse
Workflow Step: Zero FIR & Magistrate Remedies under Section 173 BNSS

1. An FIR can be registered at ANY police station irrespective of territorial jurisdiction as a 'Zero FIR', which the police station must register and transfer to the competent station.
2. If an officer refuses to register an FIR for a cognizable offence, you have the statutory right under Section 173(3) BNSS to send the complaint in writing by registered post to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or Commissioner.
3. If no action is taken within reasonable time, you can file a criminal complaint before the jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) BNSS, who can direct the police to investigate.

act: Filing a Consumer Complaint Online on e-Daakhil
clause_heading: Step-by-Step e-Daakhil Filing Process
chunk_text:
Citizen Procedural Guide: Filing a Consumer Complaint Online on e-Daakhil
Workflow Step: Step-by-Step e-Daakhil Filing Process

1. Register on edaakhil.nic.in with Aadhaar or OTP verification.
2. Select the competent District Commission based on where you reside, where the seller resides or has branch office, or where cause of action arose.
3. Upload PDF documents: Invoice/receipt, legal notice served, opposite party reply, proof of payment.
4. Pay nominal court fee online via Bharatkosh (Zero fee for claims up to ₹5 Lakhs under CPA 2019 rules).
5. The Commission will scrutinize and list the matter for admission within 21 days.

act: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal · (1997) 1 SCC 416
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 1996-12-18

ISSUE:
What mandatory guidelines and safeguards must police follow to prevent custodial torture and illegal detentions?

HOLDING:
The Supreme Court laid down 11 mandatory guidelines for arrest and detention under Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
1. Arresting officers must wear clear identification badges. 2. A memo of arrest must be prepared at the time of arrest, signed by at least one family member or respectable local witness. 3. The arrestee has the right to inform a friend or relative within 8 to 12 hours. 4. Medical examination must be conducted every 48 hours in custody by an empanelled doctor. 5. Copies of all arrest memos must be sent to the District Magistrate.

act: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar · (2014) 8 SCC 273
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2014-07-02

ISSUE:
Whether police can automatically arrest an accused in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years without recording reasons?

HOLDING:
No automatic arrest permitted in offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, including Section 498A IPC / Section 85 BNS.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Police officers must serve a notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC (now Section 35(3) BNSS) and must satisfy themselves of the necessity of arrest based on specified statutory parameters. Magistrates must not authorize detention mechanically without perusing the police officer's report.

act: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
chapter: Supreme Court of India (9-Judge Constitution Bench)
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India · (2017) 10 SCC 1
Court: Supreme Court of India (9-Judge Constitution Bench) | Date of Decision: 2017-08-24

ISSUE:
Whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution of India?

HOLDING:
Right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Privacy includes personal autonomy, informational privacy, and privacy of spatial choices. Any state encroachment on privacy must satisfy the three-fold test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.

clause_heading: Sale defined and transfer how effected
chapter: Chapter III: Of Sales of Immovable Property
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 54 (Sale defined and transfer how effected)

Sale is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised. Such transfer, in the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument. A contract for the sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties. It does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property.

clause_heading: Doctrine of Part Performance
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 53A (Doctrine of Part Performance)

Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him, and the transferee has, in part performance of the contract, taken possession of the property or any part thereof, or being already in possession, continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance of the contract, and the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract, then the transferor is debarred from enforcing against the transferee any right in respect of the property, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract. Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act mandates registration of documents containing contract for transfer of immovable property for the purpose of Section 53A.

clause_heading: Mortgage, mortgagor, mortgagee, and types of mortgages
chapter: Chapter IV: Of Mortgages of Immovable Property and Charges
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 58 (Mortgage, mortgagor, mortgagee, and types of mortgages)

A mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. The principal types include simple mortgage, mortgage by conditional sale, usufructuary mortgage, English mortgage, mortgage by deposit of title-deeds (equitable mortgage), and anomalous mortgage.

clause_heading: Gift defined and acceptance
chunk_text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · Section 122 (Gift defined and acceptance)

Gift is the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration, by one person, called the donor, to another, called the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Such acceptance must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving. Under Section 123, transfer of immovable property by gift must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses.

clause_heading: Documents of which registration is compulsory
chunk_text:
Registration Act, 1908 · Section 17 (Documents of which registration is compulsory)

The following documents shall be registered: (a) instruments of gift of immovable property; (b) other non-testamentary instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish, whether in present or in future, any right, title or interest of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, to or in immovable property; (c) non-testamentary instruments which acknowledge receipt of consideration; (d) leases of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent; (1A) documents containing contracts to transfer for consideration immovable property for Section 53A TPA purposes.

clause_heading: Effect of non-registration of documents required to be registered
chapter: Part X: Of the Effects of Registration and Non-Registration
chunk_text:
Registration Act, 1908 · Section 49 (Effect of non-registration of documents required to be registered)

No document required by Section 17 or by any provision of the Transfer of Property Act to be registered shall affect any immovable property comprised therein, or confer any power to adopt, or be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property, unless it has been registered: Provided that an unregistered document affecting immovable property may be received as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance under the Specific Relief Act or as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument.

clause_heading: Easement defined and acquisition of right of way by prescription
chunk_text:
Indian Easements Act, 1882 · Section 4 & 15 (Easement defined and acquisition of right of way by prescription)

An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own. Under Section 15, where the access and use of light or air, or right of way or other easement has been peaceably and openly enjoyed by any person claiming title thereto, as an easement and as of right, without interruption, and for twenty years, the right to such access and use shall be absolute and indefeasible. When the property belongs to the Government, the period of prescription is thirty years.

clause_heading: Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property without due process
chunk_text:
Specific Relief Act, 1963 · Section 6 (Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property without due process)

If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. No suit under this section shall be brought after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession, or against the Government. No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed.

clause_heading: Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right and perpetual injunction
chunk_text:
Specific Relief Act, 1963 · Section 34 & 38 (Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right and perpetual injunction)

Under Section 34, any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief: Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. Under Section 38, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation or where the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property.

clause_heading: Twelve-year limitation for possession based on title and adverse possession; Condonation of delay
chunk_text:
Limitation Act, 1963 · Article 65 & Section 5 (Twelve-year limitation for possession based on title and adverse possession; Condonation of delay)

Under Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, the period of limitation for a suit for possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title is twelve years. The limitation begins to run when the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff. For suits against the Government, the limitation period is thirty years under Article 112. Under Section 5, any appeal or application (other than an execution application under Order XXI CPC) may be admitted after the prescribed period if the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or application within time.

clause_heading: Functions and duties of promoter and adherence to sanctioned plans; 5-year defect liability
chapter: Chapter III: Rights and Duties of Allottees
chunk_text:
Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 · Section 11 & 14 (Functions and duties of promoter and adherence to sanctioned plans; 5-year defect liability)

Under Section 11, the promoter shall create a web page on the RERA authority website and enter project details including quarterly updates of list and number of apartments booked, approvals taken and pending, and quarterly status of the project. Under Section 14, the proposed project shall be developed and completed by the promoter in accordance with the sanctioned plans, layout plans and specifications approved by competent authorities. Any structural defect or any other defect in workmanship, quality or provision of services brought to the notice of the promoter within a period of five years from the date of handing over possession must be rectified by the promoter without further charge within thirty days.

act: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
clause_heading: Enforcement of security interest without court intervention and 60 days demand notice
chapter: Chapter III: Enforcement of Security Interest
chunk_text:
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 · Section 13 (Enforcement of security interest without court intervention and 60 days demand notice)

Notwithstanding anything contained in Section 69 or Section 69A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, any security interest created in favour of any secured creditor may be enforced, without the intervention of the court or tribunal, by such creditor. Where any borrower makes any default in repayment of secured debt and his account is classified by the secured creditor as a non-performing asset (NPA), the secured creditor may require the borrower by notice in writing to discharge in full his liabilities within sixty days from the date of notice. If the borrower fails to comply, the creditor may take possession of the secured assets under Section 13(4) or take over management.

clause_heading: Uses of agricultural land and procedure for diversion for other purposes (Land Conversion)
chapter: Chapter VIII: Grant, Use and Relinquishment of Unalienated Land
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 95 (Uses of agricultural land and procedure for diversion for other purposes (Land Conversion))

An occupant of land assessed or held for the purpose of agriculture is entitled by himself, his servants, tenants, agents or other legal representatives, to erect farm buildings, construct wells or tanks, or make other improvements for better cultivation. If any occupant wishes to divert such land or any part thereof to any other purpose (commercial, industrial, or residential), he shall apply for permission to the Deputy Commissioner. Under recent Karnataka amendments, deemed conversion applies upon submission of self-declaration and payment of prescribed conversion fine if consistent with the Master Plan published under the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961.

clause_heading: Acquisition of rights to be reported; Presumption of correctness of Record of Rights (Pahani / RTC)
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 · Section 128 & 133 (Acquisition of rights to be reported; Presumption of correctness of Record of Rights (Pahani / RTC))

Under Section 128, any person acquiring by succession, survivorship, inheritance, partition, purchase, mortgage, gift, lease or otherwise, any right as holder, occupant, owner, mortgagee, landlord or tenant of land situated in Karnataka shall report orally or in writing his acquisition of such right to the prescribed revenue officer (Tahsildar / Revenue Inspector) within three months. Under Section 133, an entry in the Record of Rights and a certified entry in the register of mutations shall be presumed to be true until the contrary is proved or a new entry is lawfully substituted. However, revenue mutation does not confer or extinguish judicial title.

clause_heading: Regulation of agricultural land acquisition and bar of jurisdiction of civil courts
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 · Section 79A, 79B & 132 (Regulation of agricultural land acquisition and bar of jurisdiction of civil courts)

Sections 79A (income limit for acquisition of agricultural land) and 79B (prohibition on holding agricultural land by non-agriculturists) of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 were omitted by Karnataka Act No. 29 of 2020. Non-agriculturists and Indian citizens are permitted to purchase agricultural land in Karnataka subject to ceiling limits under Section 63. Under Section 132, no civil court shall have jurisdiction to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under this Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Land Tribunal, Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner.

act: Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978
clause_heading: Prohibition of transfer of granted land to SC/ST persons and resumption by Assistant Commissioner
chunk_text:
Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 · Section 4 & 5 (Prohibition of transfer of granted land to SC/ST persons and resumption by Assistant Commissioner)

Under Section 4, any transfer of granted land made either before or after the commencement of this Act, in contravention of the terms of the grant or the law providing for such grant, or without prior permission of the State Government, is null and void and no right, title or interest in such land shall be conveyed. Under Section 5, the Assistant Commissioner may, on application by any interested person or on information, declare the transfer of granted land null and void, resume the land to the State Government free from all encumbrances, and restore it to the original grantee or his legal heirs.

clause_heading: Prohibition of land grabbing and Special Court jurisdiction
chunk_text:
Karnataka Land Grabbing Prohibition Act, 2011 · Section 3 & 4 (Prohibition of land grabbing and Special Court jurisdiction)

Land grabbing of any land belonging to the Government, local authority, religious or charitable institution or Wakf is declared unlawful. Any person who commits or abets land grabbing shall be punished with imprisonment for a term not less than one year which may extend to three years and with fine up to twenty-five thousand rupees. Special Courts constituted under Section 7 have exclusive jurisdiction to try offences and determine civil disputes relating to alleged government and public land grabbing.

clause_heading: Status of apartments, undivided interest in common areas and Deed of Declaration
chunk_text:
Karnataka Apartment Ownership Act, 1972 · Section 5 & 10 (Status of apartments, undivided interest in common areas and Deed of Declaration)

Each apartment owner shall be entitled to an undivided interest in the common areas and facilities in the percentage expressed in the Deed of Declaration. Such percentage cannot be altered without the consent of all apartment owners expressed in an amended Declaration. Common areas and facilities shall remain undivided, and no apartment owner or other person may bring any action for partition or division of any part thereof. Apartment Owners Associations manage maintenance, sinking funds, and compliance under registered bye-laws.

act: Bhoomi Karnataka Land Portal: Extracting RTC / Pahani and Mutation Status
section: Online Verification of Record of Rights and Mutation Register
clause_heading: Online Verification of Record of Rights and Mutation Register
chunk_text:
Citizen Procedural Guide: Bhoomi Karnataka Land Portal: Extracting RTC / Pahani and Mutation Status
Workflow Step: Online Verification of Record of Rights and Mutation Register

1. Visit the official Karnataka Bhoomi portal (bhoomi.karnataka.gov.in).
2. Navigate to 'View RTC Information' and enter District, Taluk, Hobli, Village, and Survey Number.
3. Verify Column 9 (Owner Name), Column 10 (Extent of land in Acres/Guntas), Column 11 (Khata Number), and Column 12 (Liabilities/Mortgages/Court stays).
4. Check 'Mutation Status' to track pending or disputed mutation entries filed after purchase, inheritance (Pouthi Khata), or partition.
5. Certified electronic RTC copies with digital signature can be downloaded upon paying ₹15 fee.

act: Kaveri 2.0 Karnataka Property Registration and Encumbrance Certificate (EC)
section: Encumbrance Certificate (Form 15 & 16) and Online Deed Verification
clause_heading: Encumbrance Certificate (Form 15 & 16) and Online Deed Verification
chunk_text:
Citizen Procedural Guide: Kaveri 2.0 Karnataka Property Registration and Encumbrance Certificate (EC)
Workflow Step: Encumbrance Certificate (Form 15 & 16) and Online Deed Verification

1. Access Kaveri 2.0 (kaveri.karnataka.gov.in) maintained by the Department of Stamps and Registration.
2. Search Encumbrance Certificate (EC): Select property jurisdiction, village, survey number/site number, and search window (minimum 15 to 30 years recommended).
3. Form 15 lists all registered transactions, mortgages, court attachments, and lease deeds during the searched period.
4. Form 16 (Nil Encumbrance) certifies that no registered encumbrance was found in the register for the queried period.
5. For registration: Upload draft sale deed, calculate valuation/stamp duty, book SRO appointment slot, and verify biometric Aadhaar e-KYC.

act: Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011: Guaranteed Citizen Delivery Timelines
section: Statutory Timelines for Revenue and Municipal Services
clause_heading: Statutory Timelines for Revenue and Municipal Services
chunk_text:
Citizen Procedural Guide: Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011: Guaranteed Citizen Delivery Timelines
Workflow Step: Statutory Timelines for Revenue and Municipal Services

The Karnataka Guarantee of Services to Citizens Act (Sakala) mandates fixed timelines for citizen services:
- Issuance of computerized RTC / Pahani: Same day / 3 working days.
- Mutation entry based on registered sale deed: 30 working days.
- Pouthi (Inheritance) mutation: 45 working days.
- Land Conversion under Section 95 KLRA: 60 days (or deemed approved under master plan).
- If the designated officer fails to provide service within the stipulated time, the citizen receives daily compensation deducted from the defaulting officer's salary via Sakala GSC number tracking.

act: Suraj Lamp & Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Suraj Lamp & Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Suraj Lamp & Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana · (2012) 1 SCC 656
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2011-10-11

ISSUE:
Whether sale of immovable property through General Power of Attorney (GPA), Agreement to Sell (SA), and Living Will transfers valid title?

HOLDING:
Immovable property can be legally and lawfully transferred only by a registered deed of conveyance. SA/GPA/WILL transactions do not convey any title nor do they create any interest in immovable property.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
A Power of Attorney is not an instrument of transfer in regard to any right, title or interest in an immovable property. GPA transactions cannot be recognized as deeds of title or transfer by courts or registration authorities. Such transactions do not satisfy the mandatory requirements of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act or Section 17 of the Registration Act.

clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma · (2020) 9 SCC 1
Court: Supreme Court of India (3-Judge Bench) | Date of Decision: 2020-08-11

ISSUE:
Whether the daughter's right to coparcenary property under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is conditional on the coparcener father being alive on September 9, 2005?

HOLDING:
Daughters have coparcenary rights by birth in ancestral property under amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, regardless of whether the coparcener father was alive on September 9, 2005.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
The rights conferred on daughters under Section 6 are born out of coparcenary status acquired by birth. The amendment operates on existing coparcenaries and has retroactive effect. A daughter is entitled to an equal share in coparcenary property identical to that of a son, except where a formal partition was registered before December 20, 2004.

act: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Jitendra Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh · (2021) SCC OnLine SC 802
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2021-09-06

ISSUE:
Whether mutation entry in revenue records confers ownership, title, or proprietary rights over immovable property?

HOLDING:
Mutation entry in revenue records does not confer title, ownership, or proprietary rights upon any individual; revenue records exist solely for fiscal tax collection purposes.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
It is settled law that mutation of property in the revenue records does not create or extinguish title nor has it any presumptive value on title. If there is any dispute regarding title, the parties must approach the competent Civil Court for declaration of title under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act.

act: Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur · (2019) 8 SCC 729
Court: Supreme Court of India (3-Judge Bench) | Date of Decision: 2019-08-07

ISSUE:
Whether a plea of adverse possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 can be used as a sword by the plaintiff to seek declaration of title?

HOLDING:
Adverse possession can be used as a sword by a plaintiff to declare title, not merely as a shield of defense.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
When a squatter or possessor has been in open, continuous, and hostile possession of immovable property for more than twelve years extinguishing the owner's title under Section 27 and Article 65 of the Limitation Act, he acquires a perfected title by adverse possession and can maintain an affirmative suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction.

act: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy · (2008) 4 SCC 594
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2008-03-25

ISSUE:
Under what circumstances is a bare suit for injunction maintainable, and when must a plaintiff file a comprehensive suit for declaration of title?

HOLDING:
Where a cloud is raised over the plaintiff's title and he is not in possession, or where title is seriously disputed, a suit for bare injunction is not maintainable; the remedy is a suit for declaration of title with consequential relief.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
1. Where plaintiff's title is not in dispute or under cloud, but his peaceful possession is threatened, a suit for bare permanent injunction lies. 2. Where title is disputed or clouded, plaintiff must sue for declaration of title and injunction. 3. Where plaintiff is not in possession, he must sue for declaration of title and recovery of possession.

act: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
chapter: Supreme Court of India (5-Judge Constitution Bench)
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh · (2014) 2 SCC 1
Court: Supreme Court of India (5-Judge Constitution Bench) | Date of Decision: 2013-11-12

ISSUE:
Whether a police officer is bound to register a First Information Report (FIR) upon receiving information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence?

HOLDING:
Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (now Section 173 BNSS) if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
Police officers have no discretion to refuse registration of an FIR if a cognizable offence is disclosed. Preliminary inquiry is permissible only in limited categories such as medical negligence, corruption, matrimonial/family disputes, or commercial disputes, and such inquiry must be concluded within 7 to 14 days.

clause_heading: Precedent Ratio: Rajnesh v. Neha
chunk_text:
Landmark Judgment: Rajnesh v. Neha · (2021) 2 SCC 324
Court: Supreme Court of India | Date of Decision: 2020-11-04

ISSUE:
What uniform guidelines and criteria govern the award of interim and final maintenance across matrimonial proceedings in India?

HOLDING:
The Supreme Court framed uniform national guidelines and made the submission of an Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities mandatory for both parties in all matrimonial maintenance proceedings.

RATIO DECIDENDI & BINDING PRINCIPLE:
To eliminate delays and false financial claims, both spouses must file a standardized Disclosure Affidavit detailing all assets, liabilities, bank accounts, IT returns, and lifestyle standards. Maintenance is payable from the date of filing the application.
